findings.summary: The shallow-vs-deep table is ambiguous about string columns and mixes dtype cases, so a skimming learner may misread which call is trustworthy.
findings.evidence: memory_usage() on str + pyarrow | real buffer bytes; memory_usage() on str, no pyarrow | pointers only (Python storage)
findings.fix: State the rule in one line (shallow is only reliable for fixed-width dtypes; always use deep=True for strings), and trim the table to object vs deep=True.

findings.summary: A bullet holds two ideas: the object default and the storage cost of repeated labels.
findings.evidence: pandas 3 infers str for text; object is the older default
findings.fix: Split into two bullets: the pandas 3 default dtype for text, and the point that repeated labels still store every string.

findings.summary: The overflow warning is garbled and the bullet is unclear.
findings.evidence: NumPy casts overflow wraps silently, no error
findings.fix: Rewrite as 'astype to a too-small int wraps silently, no error'.

findings.summary: Code is shown under 'Set dtypes at load' with no stated idea first, and the trailing note is detached from the code.
findings.evidence: python df = pd.read_csv('f.csv', dtype={'id': 'int32', 'tag': 'category'}, usecols=['id', 'tag']) ... full-width frame is never built
findings.fix: Put the one-line idea first: 'Set dtype and usecols at load so the full-width frame is never built', then show the code.

findings.summary: The 'Build once' idea is introduced with an ambiguous statement and the code follows before the rule is complete.
findings.evidence: concat or append per row recopies all the data ... collect in a list, build once
findings.fix: Lead with 'Collect rows in a list, build the DataFrame once' and then show the code.

findings.summary: The speed claim is vague and the table mixes rows of unlike kind.
findings.evidence: Vectorised op | compiled, whole column | 10-100x faster
findings.fix: Say 'typically much faster' or cite the source of the range, and label the table's speed column relative to the slow rows.

findings.summary: Code is shown before the idea behind the second and third lines is stated, and one code block packs three separate ideas.
findings.evidence: df['total'] = df['price'] * df['qty'] / big = df['qty'] > 5 / df['tier'] = np.where(...) / df['band'] = np.select(...)
findings.fix: Split into column math, np.where and np.select snippets, each under its own one-line idea.

findings.summary: The Polars row leaves out the 'expression API' reason from the outline.
findings.evidence: Polars | multi-core speed, lazy optimiser, ~1-100 GB, lower memory | scan_parquet, .lazy(), .collect()
findings.fix: Add 'expression API' to the Polars 'Switch when' cell, for example 'multi-core speed, lazy optimiser, expression API, ~1-100 GB, lower memory'.

findings.summary: The chained-assignment code block lists three different behaviours without saying up front which is wrong, and the text mixes several ideas per bullet.
findings.evidence: Chained assignment does nothing to df; pandas 3 warns with ChainedAssignmentError
findings.fix: Put 'Chained assignment never changes df; use .loc in one step' before the code and split the warning-name facts into their own bullet.

findings.summary: The Polars/DuckDB table packs several unrelated criteria into one cell.
findings.evidence: Polars | multi-core speed, lazy optimiser, ~1-100 GB, lower memory | scan_parquet, .lazy(), .collect()
findings.fix: Split into short one-idea bullets or separate columns for 'Pick when' and 'Key calls'.

findings.summary: The quiz poses code questions with the answer first and the code after, so 'this line' and 'What does this print' appear detached from the code.
findings.evidence: In pandas 3, what happens to df after this line, and what is the fix? ... df[df['a'] > 0]['b'] = 1
findings.fix: Place each snippet directly under its question before the answer.
